title: I built a 160ns C++20 engine for perp-to-spot adverse selection (online Hawkes process)
author: Wooden_Grass7302
selftext:
When perpetual futures get swept, spot usually follows a few milliseconds later. If you're market making on spot and your quotes are still sitting there, you get run over.

I've been building an open-source C++20 engine called **PulseLOB** to catch this lead-lag contagion in real time and turn it straight into Avellaneda–Stoikov quote skews and pulls before the lagging venue reacts.

Under the hood, it's a linear marked Hawkes process with a fixed bank of Erlang kernels (exponentials for self-excitation, Erlang-2 humps peaking at 5–20ms for cross-venue lag). Because the kernels are fixed, the online least-squares update is O(1) per event and matches the exact batch solution—verified to `2.9e-14` against a brute-force Python reference. It also runs online regime-change detection and projects parameters at every tick so the process stays sub-critical.

On an Apple M4, tick-to-quote is `0.99 µs` p50 inline (1.8M events/s) or `0.16 µs` p50 in split mode (8.4M events/s), with zero allocations on the hot path. I also wired up zero-copy Python bindings and a live Binance Spot + USD-M recorder.

Repo:[https://github.com/CodeByRachit/PulseLOB](https://github.com/CodeByRachit/PulseLOB)

Next I'm building the market-making simulator to backtest this against standard Avellaneda–Stoikov. For anyone who's traded perp/spot lead-lag or built LOB sims: do fixed Erlang-2 humps hold up well across volatility regimes, and what's the biggest realism trap I should avoid when modeling queue position and latency?
